title: Rome Is Born
text: According to legend, Romulus founded Rome on 21 April 753 BC after quarrelling with his twin brother, Remus, over where the city should go. Romans still celebrate the date every year as the Natale di Roma, the city's birthday, with parades in ancient costume.

title: Ciao Means 'Your Servant'
text: The everyday greeting ciao comes from Venetian dialect. It began as s-ciào vostro, 'I am your servant' (literally 'your slave'), a polite phrase used on meeting someone. Over the centuries it shrank to a single friendly word, now used all over the world.

title: The Spanish Steps Were French
text: Rome's famous Spanish Steps, completed in 1725, were paid for with French money to connect the square below to the French church of Trinità dei Monti at the top. They take their name from the Spanish embassy that stood in the square.

title: The First Mention of Pizza
text: The word 'pizza' first appears in a Latin document from Gaeta, south of Rome, in 997. A tenant agreed to give the local bishop twelve pizzas every Christmas and Easter. Nobody is sure what those pizzas actually looked like.

title: The Original Paparazzo
text: The word 'paparazzi' comes from Paparazzo, a pushy photographer in Federico Fellini's 1960 film La Dolce Vita. The name caught on for celebrity photographers everywhere. Fellini reportedly borrowed it from a character in an English travel book.

title: A Lab in Her Bedroom
text: Barred from university work by Fascist racial laws, Rita Levi-Montalcini built a small laboratory in her bedroom in Turin and studied chick embryos using sharpened sewing needles. Her work led to the discovery of nerve growth factor and a Nobel Prize in 1986. She lived to 103.

title: The Etruscan Puzzle
text: Before Rome dominated Italy, the Etruscans ruled much of the centre of the peninsula. We can read their alphabet, borrowed from the Greeks, and sound out their words, but their language is unrelated to its neighbours and is still only partly understood.

title: The Die Is Cast
text: In January 49 BC, Julius Caesar led his army across the Rubicon, a small river near Rimini that marked the edge of his province. Bringing troops into Italy meant civil war. He is said to have declared alea iacta est: 'the die is cast'.

title: Goodbye to the King
text: On 2 June 1946, Italians voted in a referendum to abolish the monarchy and become a republic. It was the first national vote in which Italian women could take part. The date is now a national holiday, the Festa della Repubblica.

title: The Lopsided Gondola
text: A gondola is deliberately asymmetrical: its left side is about 24 centimetres wider than its right. This counterbalances the gondolier, who stands at the back and rows on one side only, so the boat travels in a straight line.

title: Rome's Last King
text: Before it was a republic, Rome was ruled by kings, the last of them Etruscan. In 509 BC, according to Roman tradition, the Romans expelled the tyrant Tarquin the Proud and swore never to have a king again. They kept that promise for centuries, at least in name.

title: The Mona Lisa Heist
text: In August 1911, the Mona Lisa vanished from the Louvre. The thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman who believed the painting belonged in Italy. He kept it in his Paris room for two years, then tried to sell it to a dealer in Florence, who called the police.

title: Byron's Bridge of Sighs
text: The Bridge of Sighs, finished around 1600, linked the Doge's Palace to the prisons. The romantic name came later, popularised by Lord Byron in the 1800s, who imagined prisoners sighing at their last glimpse of Venice through its little stone windows.

title: The Scandalous Fork
text: Forks reached Venice in the 11th century with a Byzantine princess who married the doge Domenico Selvo and refused to eat with her fingers. Churchmen were shocked by such luxury. It took centuries for the fork to catch on in the rest of Europe.

title: An Eyewitness to Vesuvius
text: Pliny the Younger watched Vesuvius erupt from across the bay and later described it in two letters, comparing the ash cloud to an umbrella pine. Volcanologists still call this kind of eruption 'Plinian'. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, died trying to rescue people.

title: Money Doesn't Smell
text: Ancient Romans collected urine from public toilets for use in laundries and tanneries. Emperor Vespasian taxed it, and when his son complained, he held a coin to his nose and said pecunia non olet: 'money doesn't smell'. Italian public urinals are still called vespasiani.

title: The Smallest Country on Earth
text: Vatican City became an independent state on 11 February 1929, when the Lateran Treaty was signed by the Holy See and the Kingdom of Italy. At about 44 hectares, it is the smallest country in the world, roughly the size of 60 football fields.

title: Italy Unites
text: The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861, with Victor Emmanuel II as its first king. Turin was the first capital, then Florence from 1865. Rome only joined the kingdom in 1870 and became the capital the following year.

title: The Azzurri's Royal Blue
text: Italy's national teams wear blue even though it isn't on the flag. The colour, Savoy blue, honours the royal House of Savoy, which ruled when the football team first wore blue shirts in 1911. The players have been the Azzurri, 'the blues', ever since.

title: The Oldest Republic
text: Tucked inside Italy, San Marino claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic. Tradition says it was founded in 301 by Marinus, a stonemason from the island of Rab in present-day Croatia, who was fleeing the persecution of Christians.

title: Why the Giro Leader Wears Pink
text: The Giro d'Italia cycling race was first held in 1909, organised by the newspaper La Gazzetta dello Sport. Since 1931, the race leader has worn the maglia rosa, a pink jersey, to match the paper's famous pink pages.

title: Forty Days Apart
text: The word quarantine comes from the Venetian quaranta giorni, 'forty days'. During outbreaks of plague, ships arriving in Venice had to wait at anchor for forty days before anyone could come ashore. In 1423 the city also opened one of the first plague hospitals, on an island in the lagoon.

title: The Tractor Maker's Revenge
text: Ferruccio Lamborghini made his fortune building tractors. According to the story, he complained to Enzo Ferrari about the clutch on his Ferrari and was brushed off, so he decided to build better sports cars himself. Automobili Lamborghini was founded in 1963.

title: Spectacles Are Invented
text: Eyeglasses were invented in northern Italy in the late 1200s. In 1306, the friar Giordano da Pisa told a congregation in Florence that the art of making spectacles had been discovered less than twenty years earlier, and that he had met the man who invented it.

title: A Travel Book From Prison
text: Marco Polo's account of his travels in China might never have been written if he hadn't been captured during a war between Venice and Genoa. In a Genoese prison around 1298, he dictated his stories to a fellow prisoner, the writer Rustichello da Pisa.

title: The First Casino
text: In 1638, Venice opened the Ridotto, a government-run gambling house often called the world's first public casino. The word 'casino' itself is Italian, meaning 'little house', a place for gatherings and entertainment.

title: A Typewriter for a Countess
text: One of the earliest typewriters was built around 1808 by Pellegrino Turri for his friend Countess Carolina Fantoni da Fivizzano, who was losing her sight. The machine itself is lost, but letters she typed on it survive.

title: Galileo Finds New Moons
text: In January 1610, Galileo Galilei pointed his home-made telescope at Jupiter and spotted four 'stars' that moved around it night after night. They were moons. He called them the Medicean Stars to flatter the Medici, his future patrons, but we now know them as the Galilean moons.

title: A Signal Across the Atlantic
text: Guglielmo Marconi, born in Bologna in 1874, began experimenting with radio waves in his family's attic. In December 1901 he received a radio signal sent across the Atlantic, from Cornwall to Newfoundland. He shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909, aged just 35.

title: News for a Small Coin
text: The word 'gazette' comes from Venice. In the 1500s, handwritten news sheets about wars and trade were sold there, and one story is that they cost a gazeta, a small Venetian coin. Newspapers around the world are still called gazettes.

title: Months Named for Rulers
text: July is named after Julius Caesar, who reformed the calendar in 46 BC and was born in that month. August honours his heir, Augustus. Their old names were Quintilis and Sextilis, the 'fifth' and 'sixth' months of the original Roman year, which began in March.

title: The Colosseum's Real Name
text: The Colosseum opened in AD 80 under Emperor Titus with 100 days of games. Its official name was the Flavian Amphitheatre. The nickname probably came from the Colossus, a giant bronze statue of Nero that stood nearby. It could seat around 50,000 spectators.

title: The Tomato Arrives
text: Tomatoes came from the Americas and were long treated with suspicion in Europe. The first known Italian recipe for tomato sauce, 'in the Spanish style', was published in Naples in 1692 by Antonio Latini. Today it's hard to imagine Italian food without them.

title: Mozzarella and the Water Buffalo
text: Mozzarella di bufala is made from the milk of water buffalo, which have grazed the marshy plains of Campania since at least the Middle Ages. The name comes from mozzare, 'to cut off', describing how the cheese is torn into balls by hand.

title: Prosecco Is a Place
text: Prosecco takes its name from a village near Trieste, and wine from the area was praised as far back as Roman times. Since 2009, only sparkling wine from a defined zone of north-east Italy can legally be sold as Prosecco.

title: The Chip With Two Initials
text: Federico Faggin, a physicist from Vicenza, led the design of the Intel 4004, released in 1971 as the world's first commercial microprocessor. He signed his work: the initials F.F. are etched into the silicon. He went on to co-found Zilog, maker of the Z80.

title: A Mountain of Parmesan
text: Parmigiano Reggiano has been made in the same area for around 900 years, first by Benedictine and Cistercian monks. In the Decameron, written in the 1350s, Boccaccio describes an imaginary land with a mountain of grated Parmesan, where people do nothing but make pasta.

title: The Land of Calves?
text: One theory says the name Italia comes from an ancient word meaning 'land of young cattle', related to the Latin vitulus, a calf. At first the name referred only to the southern tip of the peninsula, in today's Calabria, and it gradually spread north.

title: From National Shame to Capital of Culture
text: Matera's Sassi are cave homes carved into a ravine and lived in for thousands of years. In the 1950s their poverty was called a national disgrace and residents were moved out. Restored, the town was named a European Capital of Culture for 2019.

title: A Republic for 1,100 Years
text: According to tradition, Venice elected its first doge in 697. The Most Serene Republic lasted about 1,100 years, trading across the Mediterranean, until Napoleon's army arrived in 1797 and the last doge, Ludovico Manin, stepped down.

title: The Pantheon's Concrete Dome
text: The Pantheon was rebuilt under Emperor Hadrian around AD 125. Nearly 2,000 years later, its dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. The hole at the top, the oculus, is almost nine metres wide and is the building's only window.

title: The Broken Bench
text: Medieval Italian money-changers did business at a bench, or banco, which gave us the word 'bank'. 'Bankrupt' comes from banca rotta, a 'broken bench'. The oldest bank still operating today, Monte dei Paschi di Siena, was founded in 1472.

title: The Medieval Manhattan
text: The Tuscan hill town of San Gimignano once had around 72 towers, built by rival families trying to outdo each other. Fourteen still stand, which has earned it the nickname the medieval Manhattan.

title: Michelangelo's Only Signature
text: The Pietà in St Peter's Basilica is the only work Michelangelo ever signed. According to the biographer Vasari, he overheard visitors credit it to another sculptor, so he came back at night and carved his name across the Virgin's sash.

title: The Violin Master
text: Antonio Stradivari made violins, violas and cellos in Cremona for more than 60 years. Around 650 of his instruments survive, and the finest have sold for more than 15 million US dollars. Scientists still argue over what makes them sound so good.

title: The Oldest University
text: The University of Bologna dates itself to 1088, which makes it the oldest university in the Western world. It began as a gathering of students who hired teachers to instruct them in law. Petrarch and Copernicus both studied there.

title: The Desktop Computer That Went to the Moon
text: Olivetti's Programma 101, unveiled in 1965, is often called the first commercially available desktop computer. It stored programs on magnetic cards, and NASA used it for calculations during the Apollo 11 mission. A small team in Ivrea led by Pier Giorgio Perotto designed it.

title: Hollywood on the Tiber
text: Cinecittà, Rome's film studio complex, opened in 1937. After the war, so many American productions filmed there, including Ben-Hur in 1959, that it became known as Hollywood on the Tiber. Federico Fellini made most of his films there.

title: The 'New City'
text: Naples began as a Greek colony. Its name comes from the Greek Neapolis, 'new city', founded beside an older settlement called Parthenope. Greek was still spoken in the city long after it came under Roman rule.

title: Gelato for the Medici
text: Florentine legend credits the architect Bernardo Buontalenti with serving an early gelato at the Medici court in the 1500s. In 1686 a Sicilian, Francesco Procopio dei Coltelli, opened the Café Procope in Paris, where his ices helped make Italian frozen desserts famous.

title: Glassmakers Sent to an Island
text: In 1291, Venice ordered its glass furnaces moved to the island of Murano, partly to protect the wooden city from fire. Murano's glassmakers became celebrated, but they were also forbidden to leave the Republic, so that their secrets stayed in Venice.

title: A Warship Before Dessert
text: Venice's Arsenale was one of the largest industrial sites in pre-industrial Europe, building ships in an early form of assembly line. In 1574, its workers reportedly put together a complete galley while King Henry III of France sat through a banquet.

title: Fibonacci Brings Numbers
text: In 1202, Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, published the Liber Abaci, introducing Europe to the Hindu-Arabic numerals 0 to 9 that he had seen traders use in North Africa. The book also contained a puzzle about breeding rabbits that gives us the Fibonacci sequence.

title: The Last Supper Survives a Bomb
text: Leonardo painted The Last Supper on a dry wall instead of wet plaster, so it began flaking within his lifetime. In August 1943, a bomb destroyed much of the monastery around it, but the wall survived, protected by sandbags and scaffolding.

title: David From a Rejected Block
text: Michelangelo carved his David from a huge block of marble that other sculptors had started and abandoned decades earlier. He was 26 when he began. The finished statue, over five metres tall, was meant for the cathedral roof but was placed in the city's main square instead.

title: The Prancing Horse
text: Ferrari's prancing horse first appeared on the plane of Francesco Baracca, Italy's top fighter pilot of the First World War. In 1923, Baracca's mother suggested Enzo Ferrari use it for luck. Ferrari added the yellow background, the colour of his home town, Modena.

title: Reading Scrolls Burned by Vesuvius
text: The eruption of AD 79 carbonised a library of papyrus scrolls in a villa at Herculaneum. In 2023, a student used machine learning on X-ray scans to read the first word from inside a scroll that had never been unrolled. It was the Greek word for 'purple'.

title: The First Nativity Scene
text: On Christmas Eve 1223, Saint Francis of Assisi set up a manger with a live ox and donkey in a cave at Greccio, so people could picture the birth of Christ. It is remembered as the first nativity scene, the start of Italy's beloved presepe tradition.

title: Fermi and the First Reactor
text: Enrico Fermi, born in Rome, won the Nobel Prize in 1938 and used the trip to Stockholm to leave Fascist Italy, whose new racial laws threatened his Jewish wife. In 1942 in Chicago, his team built and ran the world's first nuclear reactor.

title: Coins in the Fountain
text: The Trevi Fountain was completed in 1762. Tradition says a coin tossed over your shoulder into it means you will return to Rome. Visitors throw in more than a million euros a year, which the city collects and gives to the charity Caritas.

title: The Lighthouse of the Mediterranean
text: The volcano on the island of Stromboli has been erupting almost continuously for around 2,000 years, throwing up bursts of glowing lava every few minutes. Sailors used it to navigate at night, which earned it the nickname the Lighthouse of the Mediterranean.

title: The Pizza Fit for a Queen
text: In June 1889, Naples pizzaiolo Raffaele Esposito is said to have made a pizza for Queen Margherita of Savoy in the colours of the new Italian flag: red tomato, white mozzarella and green basil. Historians argue over the details, but the name Margherita stuck.

title: The Espresso Machine
text: In 1884, Angelo Moriondo of Turin patented a steam-powered machine for making coffee quickly and in bulk. In the late 1940s, Achille Gaggia's lever machines forced water through the grounds at high pressure, creating the golden crema that defines espresso today.

title: A Continent Named After a Florentine
text: The Florentine navigator Amerigo Vespucci argued that the lands across the Atlantic were a new continent, not part of Asia. In 1507, the German mapmaker Martin Waldseemüller labelled it 'America' in his honour, and the name stuck.

title: An Apology to Galileo
text: In 1633, the Inquisition forced Galileo to renounce his view that the Earth moves around the Sun, and he spent his final years under house arrest. In 1992, Pope John Paul II formally acknowledged that the Church had been wrong to condemn him.

title: Bologna's Skyline of Towers
text: In the Middle Ages, Bologna's wealthy families built tall towers as fortresses and status symbols, and there may have been around 100 of them. About 20 survive, including the Asinelli Tower, 97 metres tall, and its leaning neighbour, the Garisenda.

title: Elephants in the Alps
text: In 218 BC, the Carthaginian general Hannibal crossed the Alps into Italy with an army that included around 37 war elephants. Few of the elephants survived the cold, but Hannibal won crushing victories and fought on in Italy for 15 years.

title: Dante Writes in Italian
text: Dante Alighieri wrote the Divine Comedy in everyday Tuscan rather than Latin, the language of scholars. The poem was so widely read that Florentine became the basis of modern standard Italian, which is why Dante is often called the father of the Italian language.

title: A Lottery Born From Elections
text: Italy's Lotto has roots in 16th-century Genoa, where citizens placed bets on which candidates would be drawn to serve on the city's governing council. The betting proved so popular that it was eventually run with numbers instead of names.

title: The Father of Accounting
text: In 1494, the Franciscan friar Luca Pacioli published, in Venice, the first printed explanation of double-entry bookkeeping, the system used by Venetian merchants. Pacioli was also a friend of Leonardo da Vinci and taught him mathematics.

title: Galileo's Finger
text: When Galileo's body was moved to a grand tomb in Florence in 1737, admirers removed a few souvenirs, including the middle finger of his right hand. It is now displayed in a glass case at the Museo Galileo, pointing towards the sky.

title: Bankers to the Popes
text: The Medici started as bankers in Florence and became one of the most powerful families in Europe. They paid artists like Botticelli and Michelangelo, ruled Florence for generations, and produced popes, including Leo X and Clement VII, and two queens of France.

title: Music Speaks Italian
text: Musicians everywhere write piano, forte, allegro and crescendo because Italy led European music in the 1600s and 1700s. Italian composers and music printers set the standard, and their words for speed and volume became the international language of sheet music.

title: The Wasp
text: Piaggio launched the Vespa scooter in 1946 to get post-war Italy moving cheaply. On seeing the prototype, with its narrow waist and buzzing engine, Enrico Piaggio reportedly said it looked like a wasp, a vespa. The film Roman Holiday made it a star in 1953.

title: Thousands of Stone Towers
text: Sardinia is dotted with nuraghi, cone-shaped stone towers built from around 1800 BC by the island's Bronze Age people. Thousands survive, and the largest complex, Su Nuraxi at Barumini, is a World Heritage Site. Archaeologists still debate exactly what they were for.

title: Pinocchio's Debut
text: Carlo Collodi's Adventures of Pinocchio first appeared in instalments in a Roman children's magazine in 1881, and as a book in 1883. In the original story, the wooden puppet is far naughtier than in most later film versions.

title: One Bridge for 300 Years
text: The stone Rialto Bridge was completed in 1591. It replaced a series of wooden bridges, one of which collapsed under a crowd watching a wedding procession. For almost three centuries it was the only way to cross the Grand Canal on foot.

title: Ravenna's Glittering Mosaics
text: Ravenna became capital of the Western Roman Empire in 402, and later a Byzantine stronghold. Its churches are covered in gold and glass mosaics, including portraits of Emperor Justinian and Empress Theodora that are around 1,500 years old.

title: A Nation Learning Its Language
text: When Italy was unified in 1861, most Italians spoke regional dialects at home. Estimates suggest only 2.5 to 10 per cent could speak standard Italian. Schools, newspapers, the army and, later, radio and television slowly spread a shared national language.

title: Opera Is Born
text: Opera was invented in Italy around 1600 by Florentine musicians trying to revive ancient Greek drama. Claudio Monteverdi's L'Orfeo, first performed in Mantua in 1607, is the earliest opera still regularly staged today.

title: The Venetian Who Reached Canada
text: Giovanni Caboto, a Venetian citizen, sailed from Bristol in 1497 for King Henry VII of England and reached the coast of North America, probably Newfoundland. The English knew him as John Cabot.

title: The Oldest Film Festival
text: The Venice Film Festival was first held in 1932 on the terrace of the Hotel Excelsior on the Lido, making it the oldest film festival in the world. Its top prize is the Golden Lion, after the winged lion of Saint Mark, the symbol of Venice.

title: Where 'Ghetto' Comes From
text: In 1516, Venice forced its Jewish residents to live on a small island in the Cannaregio district, the site of an old copper foundry, or getto. The word 'ghetto' spread from there. The area still has historic synagogues and a Jewish community today.

title: The Thousand Red Shirts
text: In May 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi landed at Marsala in Sicily with about a thousand volunteers in red shirts. Within months they had taken Sicily and Naples, and Garibaldi handed southern Italy to King Victor Emmanuel II, making unification possible.

title: Michelangelo Stood Up
text: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512 for Pope Julius II. Contrary to legend, he worked standing on scaffolding, craning his neck backwards. He wrote a comic poem complaining that his beard pointed at the sky and paint dripped onto his face.

title: Soft and Loud
text: The piano was invented around 1700 by Bartolomeo Cristofori, keeper of instruments for the Medici in Florence. He called it a gravicembalo col piano e forte: a harpsichord that played soft or loud depending on how hard you struck the keys. The name was later shortened to 'piano'.

title: A Dome Without Scaffolding
text: Florence's cathedral had a gaping hole in its roof for decades because no one knew how to cover it. Filippo Brunelleschi built the dome without the usual wooden supports, using clever herringbone brickwork. Completed in 1436, it is still the largest brick dome ever built.

title: Birth of the Tricolore
text: The green, white and red flag was first adopted as a national flag on 7 January 1797 by the Cispadane Republic, meeting in Reggio Emilia. Italy celebrates the date every year as Tricolour Day, the Festa del Tricolore.

title: An Island Ruled by Everyone
text: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean. Over the centuries it was ruled by Greeks, Carthaginians, Romans, Byzantines, Arabs, Normans and Spaniards, and each left traces in its buildings, its dialect and its food.

title: The Queen of Roads
text: The Via Appia, begun in 312 BC by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, ran from Rome to Capua and was later extended to Brindisi on the heel of Italy. Romans called it the regina viarum, the queen of roads, and stretches of its original paving can still be walked today.

title: Pasta Before Marco Polo
text: A popular myth says Marco Polo brought pasta back from China. But in 1154, more than a century before his journey, the Arab geographer al-Idrisi described Trabia, a town near Palermo, making dried pasta and shipping it around the Mediterranean.

title: Pompeii's Autumn Surprise
text: For centuries, Vesuvius was said to have buried Pompeii on 24 August AD 79. But autumn fruit had long turned up in the ruins, and in 2018 archaeologists found a charcoal inscription dated to mid-October. Many historians now think the eruption happened in autumn.

title: A Horse Race With Few Rules
text: Siena's Palio is run twice a year, on 2 July and 16 August, around the city's sloping main square. Ten of the city's 17 districts race bareback horses for about 90 seconds, and a horse can win even after throwing its rider.

title: The Swiss Guard
text: The Pope's bodyguards, the Pontifical Swiss Guard, have protected the Vatican since 1506, when Pope Julius II hired 150 Swiss soldiers. Recruits must still be Swiss Catholic men, and they wear striped uniforms in blue, red and yellow.

title: Who Made Tiramisu?
text: Tiramisu, 'pick me up', is younger than many people think. It appeared in restaurants in the Veneto in the 1960s and 70s, and Le Beccherie in Treviso is often credited. Neighbouring Friuli Venezia Giulia disputes the claim, and the argument still goes on.

title: The First Woman Doctor of Philosophy
text: On 25 June 1678, Elena Lucrezia Cornaro Piscopia received a doctorate in philosophy from the University of Padua, the first woman known to earn a university doctorate. So many people came to watch that the ceremony was moved from the university to the cathedral.

title: A Coffee Named After Friars
text: The cappuccino is named after the Capuchin friars, whose brown hooded robes matched the colour of coffee mixed with milk. The friars themselves were named after their pointed hood, the cappuccio.

title: Meucci's Telephone
text: Florence-born Antonio Meucci developed a voice-communication device in New York in the 1850s, but couldn't afford to renew his patent caveat. In 2002, the US House of Representatives passed a resolution honouring his work on the invention of the telephone.

title: Mountains Named After a Frenchman
text: The Dolomites are named after Déodat de Dolomieu, a French geologist who studied their unusual rock in the 1790s. The mineral was named dolomite in his honour, and the mountains took the name too.

title: A Tower That Leaned From the Start
text: Work on Pisa's bell tower began in 1173, and it started to tilt after only three storeys because the ground beneath was soft clay and sand. Wars paused construction for decades, which luckily let the soil settle. Engineers straightened it by about 40 cm between 1990 and 2001.

title: The Last Emperor of the West
text: In 476, the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna. The date usually marks the end of the Western Roman Empire, and the last emperor's name, by coincidence, echoed both Rome's founder and its first emperor.

title: A Student's Anthem
text: Italy's national anthem, Il Canto degli Italiani, was written in 1847 by Goffredo Mameli, a 20-year-old student who died two years later fighting for the Roman Republic. It was used provisionally from 1946 and only became the official anthem by law in 2017.

title: Arab Sicily's Gifts
text: During more than two centuries of Arab rule, Sicily gained new irrigation systems and new crops, including citrus fruit, sugar cane and rice. Sicilian classics like arancini, cassata and granita owe a great deal to that period.

title: The First Battery
text: In 1800, Alessandro Volta of Como stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by cloth soaked in salt water, creating the first electric battery, the voltaic pile. Napoleon was so impressed he later made Volta a count. The volt is named after him.

title: Carnival Behind a Mask
text: Masks let Venetians of every class mix freely during Carnevale. After the Republic fell in 1797 the festival faded, and masks were restricted under foreign rule. It was only fully revived in 1979, and now draws huge crowds each winter before Lent.

title: The Doctor Who Changed School
text: Maria Montessori was one of the first women to qualify as a doctor in Italy. In 1907 she opened her first Casa dei Bambini, a children's house, in a poor Rome neighbourhood, where her child-led teaching methods were born. Montessori schools now exist all over the world.

title: Houses You Could Take Apart
text: Alberobello in Puglia is famous for its trulli, whitewashed stone huts with cone-shaped roofs, built without mortar. A popular story says the dry-stone design let owners quickly dismantle them to dodge taxes on new buildings.

title: Nutella's Wartime Roots
text: After the Second World War, chocolate was scarce and expensive in Italy. In 1946, Pietro Ferrero, a pastry maker in Alba, stretched it with local Piedmont hazelnuts to make an affordable paste. His family relaunched the recipe as Nutella in 1964.

title: Ötzi the Iceman
text: In 1991, hikers in the Alps near the Italian-Austrian border found a body in the ice. It was a man who had died about 5,300 years earlier, still with his copper axe, bow and clothes. Ötzi had more than 60 tattoos and now rests in a museum in Bolzano.

title: Leonardo's Mirror Writing
text: Leonardo da Vinci filled thousands of notebook pages in mirror writing, running from right to left. He was left-handed, and writing backwards may have stopped the ink smudging. In 1994 one notebook, the Codex Leicester, sold for over 30 million US dollars.

title: Saved by the Geese
text: When Gauls tried to scale the Capitoline Hill by night, the dogs stayed quiet but the sacred geese of Juno honked and flapped. Their racket woke the former consul Marcus Manlius, who threw the first attacker back down the cliff and saved the citadel.

title: Back to the Plough
text: Cincinnatus was ploughing his small farm when messengers arrived to make him dictator and save Rome from an invading army. He won the war in about two weeks, gave up absolute power, and went straight back to his fields.

title: Laws on Bronze Tablets
text: Rome's first written laws, the Twelve Tables, were put on display in the Forum so every citizen could read them. Roman schoolboys still had to learn them by heart centuries later, long after the original tablets were lost.

title: The Great Drain
text: The Cloaca Maxima, Rome's 'greatest sewer', was begun under the city's early kings to drain the marshy valley where the Forum now stands. Parts of it still carry water to the Tiber, more than 2,500 years later.

title: Water by the Mile
text: Rome's first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, was built in 312 BC by Appius Claudius, the same man behind the Appian Way. By the 200s AD, eleven aqueducts brought the city so much water that fountains ran day and night.

title: All Roads Lead to Rome
text: Augustus set up a gilded column in the Forum, the Golden Milestone, listing the distances to the empire's great cities. It was treated as the point where Rome's roads began, and it's often linked to the saying 'all roads lead to Rome'.

title: The Year of Confusion
text: Rome's calendar had drifted so far from the seasons that Julius Caesar fixed it with a 365-day year and a leap day every four years. To catch up, 46 BC was stretched to 445 days, and Romans called it the year of confusion.

title: Beware the Ides of March
text: Julius Caesar was stabbed by a group of senators on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BC, at a meeting hall built by his old rival Pompey. Its ruins are in today's Largo di Torre Argentina, now a famous sanctuary for stray cats.

title: A City of Marble
text: The historian Suetonius wrote that Augustus boasted he had found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble. During his reign, new quarries at Carrara supplied the gleaming white stone for temples, forums and theatres.

title: Bread and Circuses
text: The poet Juvenal complained that the Roman people, who once handed out armies and high office, now longed for only two things: bread and circuses. His phrase, panem et circenses, is still used for keeping people happy with handouts and shows.

title: The Biggest Racetrack
text: The Circus Maximus, where Romans watched chariot races, could hold some 150,000 spectators. Four colour-coded teams, the Reds, Whites, Greens and Blues, had fans as passionate as any football crowd. The last races were held in AD 549.

title: Spartacus Breaks Free
text: Spartacus and about seventy gladiators escaped a training school near Capua armed with kitchen knives. Their revolt grew into an army of tens of thousands of slaves that beat several Roman forces before it was crushed in 71 BC.

title: Nero Didn't Fiddle
text: When the Great Fire of Rome broke out in AD 64, Nero was at his villa in Antium, about 50 kilometres away. The story that he fiddled while Rome burned can't be true, because the fiddle hadn't been invented yet.

title: A Horse in the Senate?
text: The emperor Caligula loved his racehorse Incitatus so much that he gave it a marble stall, an ivory manger and servants. Ancient writers claimed he even planned to make it a consul, though that may have been a joke to insult the Senate.

title: A Story Told in Spiral
text: Trajan's Column is wrapped in a carved band about 200 metres long, showing his wars in Dacia, modern Romania, with some 2,500 figures. Inside, a spiral staircase still climbs to the top, where a statue of St Peter replaced Trajan in 1587.

title: The Mouth of Truth
text: The Bocca della Verità is a huge marble face, probably an ancient drain cover. Legend says it bites off the hand of anyone who tells a lie while their hand is in its mouth, a scene Gregory Peck played for laughs in Roman Holiday in 1953.

title: Graffiti in Pompeii
text: Pompeii's walls are covered with thousands of scratched messages: election slogans, love notes, insults and jokes. One reads, roughly, 'Wall, I'm amazed you haven't collapsed under the weight of so much rubbish written on you.'

title: The Romans' Ketchup
text: Romans splashed garum, a salty sauce of fermented fish, on almost everything. Pompeii had workshops making it, and one producer, Umbricius Scaurus, decorated his house with mosaics of garum jars bearing his own name.

title: Concrete That Gets Stronger
text: Roman engineers mixed volcanic ash from around Pozzuoli into their concrete. In seawater it slowly forms new minerals, which is why Roman harbour walls have lasted 2,000 years while many modern ones crumble in decades.

title: Keepers of the Flame
text: The Vestal Virgins tended the sacred fire of Vesta in the Forum, which was never allowed to go out. They served for thirty years, had rare privileges such as their own seats at the games, and could even pardon a prisoner they passed.

title: The Original Christmas Party
text: Every December, Romans celebrated Saturnalia with feasting, gift-giving and candles. Schools closed, gambling was allowed, and masters sometimes served dinner to their slaves. Many of its customs live on in Christmas celebrations.

title: Eureka in Syracuse
text: The Greek genius Archimedes defended his home city of Syracuse against Rome with cranes and catapults. When the city fell, he was killed by a Roman soldier, supposedly while drawing circles in the sand and asking not to be disturbed.

title: Greek Temples in Campania
text: South of Salerno stand three Greek temples that are among the best preserved anywhere, older than the Parthenon in Athens. The town was founded by Greek settlers as Poseidonia, the city of Poseidon, and later renamed Paestum by the Romans.

title: Life Like a Sybarite
text: The Greek city of Sybaris in Calabria was so rich that its people became bywords for luxury. Stories claimed they banned noisy trades and invented the first patents for recipes. A pleasure-seeker is still called a sybarite.

title: The Valley of the Temples
text: Agrigento, called Akragas by the Greeks, was one of the grandest cities of the ancient world. Its ridge of temples, including the remarkably complete Temple of Concordia, glows gold at sunset above the almond trees.

title: The Boat Houses of Herculaneum
text: For years, archaeologists wondered why so few bodies were found in Herculaneum. Then, in the 1980s, they dug down to the ancient shoreline and found around 300 skeletons in the boat houses, where people had sheltered hoping to be rescued by sea.

title: In This Sign, Conquer
text: Before the battle of the Milvian Bridge, the emperor Constantine is said to have seen a sign in the sky telling him he would win under the sign of Christ. He won, and the next year his edict gave Christians freedom to worship.

title: The First Million
text: At its height, ancient Rome probably had around a million people, making it the largest city in the world. No European city would be as big again until London, more than 1,500 years later.

title: A Pyramid in Rome
text: A white pyramid stands beside one of Rome's old gates. It's the tomb of Gaius Cestius, a Roman magistrate who caught the craze for all things Egyptian after Egypt became part of the empire. It took 330 days to build.

title: The Philosopher on Horseback
text: The bronze statue of Marcus Aurelius on horseback survived when almost all others were melted down, because people in the Middle Ages thought it showed Constantine, the first Christian emperor. The original is now in the Capitoline Museums.

title: A Sponge on a Stick
text: Roman public toilets were sociable places, with long stone benches and no partitions. Instead of paper, people used a sea sponge on a stick, rinsed in a channel of running water. The latrines at Ostia Antica can still be seen today.

title: The First Encyclopedia
text: Pliny the Elder's Natural History gathered everything Romans knew about the world, from stars to stones, in 37 books. Pliny died two years later at Vesuvius, after sailing across the bay to rescue friends and get a closer look at the eruption.

title: Save the Aeneid
text: The poet Virgil died at Brindisi before he had finished polishing the Aeneid, his epic of Rome's origins, and asked for it to be burned. The emperor Augustus refused, and the poem became the most famous work in Latin.

title: Fast Food in Pompeii
text: Pompeii had dozens of street-food counters called thermopolia, with clay pots set into the counter. One uncovered in 2020 still had traces of duck, pork, fish and snails, and a painting of a chicken on the front, a sort of ancient menu.

title: Rome's Apartment Blocks
text: Most Romans lived in insulae, apartment blocks several storeys high. Rents went down as you went up, because the top floors had no water and were the hardest to escape in a fire. Augustus limited their height to about 20 metres.

title: The Stone Roof
text: Theodoric, the Ostrogoth king who ruled Italy from Ravenna, built a mausoleum topped with a single piece of stone about ten metres across, weighing some 230 tonnes. How it was lifted into place is still debated.

title: Lombards Name a Region
text: In 568 the Lombards, a Germanic people from the north, swept into Italy and made Pavia their capital. They ruled much of the peninsula for two centuries and left their name on Lombardy.

title: An Emperor for Christmas
text: On Christmas Day in the year 800, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne as emperor in St Peter's Basilica. It was the first time a western emperor had been crowned in three centuries.

title: Europe's First Medical School
text: The Schola Medica Salernitana drew students from across Europe and taught medicine from Greek, Latin, Arabic and Jewish sources. Women studied and taught there too, including Trota, whose writings on women's health were read for centuries.

title: The Wonder of the World
text: Emperor Frederick II, who grew up in Palermo, spoke several languages and wrote a book on falconry, was called Stupor Mundi, the wonder of the world. His Castel del Monte in Puglia is an eight-sided castle with eight eight-sided towers.

title: The Sicilian Vespers
text: As the bells rang for evening prayers on Easter Monday, 1282, Palermo rose up against its French rulers. The revolt spread across Sicily within weeks. Verdi later turned the story into an opera, I vespri siciliani.

title: Brother Sun, Sister Moon
text: St Francis of Assisi's Canticle of the Creatures praises God for 'brother sun', 'sister moon' and 'sister water'. Written in his local Umbrian dialect, it is one of the oldest surviving poems in the Italian language.

title: The Laws of the Sea
text: Amalfi was once a maritime republic whose ships traded across the Mediterranean. Its sea code, the Tavole Amalfitane, governed shipping for centuries. Amalfi still races Venice, Genoa and Pisa in an annual regatta of the old republics.

title: Smuggled Under Pork
text: Two Venetian merchants stole the body of St Mark from Alexandria and, the story goes, hid it under layers of pork so Muslim customs officials wouldn't search the basket. St Mark and his winged lion became the symbols of Venice.

title: Horses That Travelled Far
text: The four bronze horses of St Mark's were taken from Constantinople by Venetian crusaders in 1204. Napoleon carried them off to Paris in 1797, and they came back in 1815. The originals are now kept indoors, with copies on the facade.

title: The Golden Florin
text: Florence minted the florin in 1252, a gold coin stamped with a lily and John the Baptist. It held its value so well that it became the dollar of medieval Europe, and other countries copied it.

title: Goldsmiths on the Bridge
text: The Ponte Vecchio was once lined with butchers who threw scraps into the Arno. In 1593 Grand Duke Ferdinando I ordered them out and let in goldsmiths instead. It was the only Florence bridge the retreating Germans didn't blow up in 1944.

title: Six Centuries to Finish
text: Work on Milan's cathedral began in 1386 and the last bronze doors went up in 1965. Its roof bristles with more than 3,400 statues, and the gilded Madonnina on the top spire has watched over the city since 1774.

title: A City of Porticoes
text: Bologna has more than 60 kilometres of covered arcades, so you can walk across town in the rain without an umbrella. The longest runs nearly four kilometres up a hill to the Sanctuary of San Luca. They became a World Heritage Site in 2021.

title: Victory at Legnano
text: In 1176 the cities of the Lombard League defeated the emperor Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano. The battle became a symbol of Italian freedom and is still named in the national anthem: 'from the Alps to Sicily, wherever is Legnano'.

title: Barefoot in the Snow
text: After falling out with Pope Gregory VII, the emperor Henry IV stood barefoot in the snow outside Canossa castle for three days to beg forgiveness. 'Going to Canossa' still means swallowing your pride.

title: Do, Re, Mi
text: The monk Guido of Arezzo taught singers new melodies by naming the notes after the first syllables of a Latin hymn: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. Ut later became do. He also helped popularise writing music on lines, the ancestor of the modern stave.

title: A Calendar Fixed in Italy
text: By the 1500s, Caesar's calendar was ten days out of step with the sun. Pope Gregory XIII adopted a fix worked out largely by the Calabrian doctor Luigi Lilio, and in Italy Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October.

title: The Plague and the Decameron
text: The Black Death killed perhaps half of Florence's people in 1348. Giovanni Boccaccio set his Decameron in that year: ten young people escape to a villa in the hills and pass the time by telling each other a hundred stories.

title: The Father of Humanism
text: Francesco Petrarca, known in English as Petrarch, hunted for lost Latin manuscripts and wrote hundreds of poems to a woman he called Laura. His sonnets shaped European love poetry for centuries. He spent his last years in the hill village of Arquà, near Padua.

title: Giotto's Perfect Circle
text: When a papal messenger asked Giotto for a sample of his work, the painter is said to have dipped his brush in red and drawn a perfect circle freehand. The messenger was baffled, but the pope understood, and Giotto got the job.

title: A Fresco About Good Government
text: In Siena's town hall, Ambrogio Lorenzetti painted the effects of good and bad government. Under good rule, merchants trade, builders work and people dance in the street. Under bad rule, the city crumbles. The councillors met right beneath it.

title: The Field of Miracles
text: The lawn around Pisa's cathedral, baptistery and leaning tower is known as the Piazza dei Miracoli. The name comes from the poet Gabriele D'Annunzio, who described it as a meadow of miracles in a novel published in 1910.

title: Born in Genoa
text: Christopher Columbus, Cristoforo Colombo in Italian, was born in Genoa, the son of a wool weaver. He sailed for Spain in 1492, after Portugal had turned his plan down. Genoa's airport is now named after him.

title: The Gates of Paradise
text: Lorenzo Ghiberti spent 27 years on a pair of gilded bronze doors for Florence's baptistery, with ten panels of Bible stories. Michelangelo is said to have called them fit to be the gates of paradise, and the name stuck.

title: Brunelleschi's Peephole
text: To prove his method of perspective, Filippo Brunelleschi painted the baptistery on a panel with a small hole in it. Viewers looked through the back of the hole at a mirror reflecting the painting, and it lined up perfectly with the real building.

title: Murder at Mass
text: During Sunday Mass in Florence cathedral, members of the Pazzi family attacked the Medici brothers. Giuliano was killed, but Lorenzo escaped into the sacristy. The plotters were hanged, and Lorenzo the Magnificent's grip on Florence only grew stronger.

title: The Bonfire of the Vanities
text: The fiery friar Savonarola had Florentines burn mirrors, cosmetics, playing cards and paintings in the main square. Some say Botticelli threw in a few of his own works. A year later, Savonarola himself was executed in the same square.

title: The Prince
text: Out of a job and banished from Florence, Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince at his farmhouse south of the city. In a famous letter he described changing out of his muddy clothes each evening into courtly robes to talk with the great writers of the past.

title: Leonardo's Job Application
text: Seeking work with the Duke of Milan, Leonardo da Vinci wrote a letter listing what he could do: portable bridges, siege engines, cannons, armoured cars. Only near the end did he mention that he could also paint.

title: The Horse That Was Never Cast
text: Leonardo made a clay model, more than seven metres tall, for a giant bronze horse in Milan. The bronze set aside for it was used for cannons instead, and when the French took the city in 1499 their archers used the model for target practice.

title: Raphael in the Pantheon
text: Raphael died in 1520, aged just 37, at the height of his fame. At his own request he was buried in the Pantheon. His tomb carries a Latin verse saying that while he lived, nature feared he would outdo her.

title: The Painter on the Run
text: Caravaggio painted saints and sinners with dramatic light and real Roman street people as models. After killing a man in a brawl in 1606 he fled Rome, painting his way through Naples, Malta and Sicily, and died before he could return.

title: Artemisia Breaks In
text: Artemisia Gentileschi became the first woman admitted to Florence's Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. Her powerful paintings of heroines like Judith were admired by kings, and she ran her own successful workshop in Naples.

title: A Painter for a King
text: Sofonisba Anguissola, the eldest of six talented sisters from Cremona, was praised by Michelangelo and became court painter to Philip II of Spain. She lived into her nineties, and the young Anthony van Dyck visited to sketch her.

title: The Swinging Lamp
text: The story goes that, as a young student in Pisa cathedral, Galileo timed a swinging lamp against his pulse and saw that each swing took the same time, wide or narrow. The discovery led eventually to the pendulum clock.

title: Weighing the Air
text: Galileo's pupil Evangelista Torricelli filled a glass tube with mercury, turned it upside down in a dish and saw the mercury drop, leaving an empty space at the top. He had made the first barometer, and the first lasting vacuum.

title: Pocket Books and Italics
text: The Venetian printer Aldus Manutius began publishing the classics in small, cheap editions that could be carried around, the ancestors of the paperback. To fit more on a page he used a new slanted typeface, which English still calls italic.

title: Just the Offices
text: The Uffizi, one of the world's great art galleries, was built by Giorgio Vasari to house the Medici government's offices. That's all its name means: uffizi is old Florentine for 'offices'.

title: Palladio's Villas
text: Andrea Palladio began as a stonemason and became the most copied architect in history. His temple-fronted villas around Vicenza inspired country houses across England and, through Thomas Jefferson, buildings all over America.

title: The Fountain of Four Rivers
text: In Bernini's fountain in Piazza Navona, giant figures stand for the Danube, Ganges, Nile and Río de la Plata. Legend says one shields his eyes from Borromini's church opposite, but the church was built after the fountain.

title: 120 Years of Building
text: The new St Peter's Basilica took 120 years to build and passed through the hands of Bramante, Raphael, Michelangelo, Maderno and more. Michelangelo designed the great dome but didn't live to see it finished.

title: Black Smoke, White Smoke
text: When cardinals meet in the Sistine Chapel to elect a pope, their ballots are burned after each vote. Black smoke from the chimney means no decision yet; white smoke means there's a new pope. Since 2005 the bells of St Peter's ring too.

title: Harlequin and Friends
text: Commedia dell'arte troupes toured Europe improvising comedies with stock masked characters: the clever servant Harlequin, the greedy old Pantalone, the boastful Captain and the Neapolitan Pulcinella, who became Mr Punch in England.

title: The Red Priest
text: Antonio Vivaldi, nicknamed the Red Priest for his hair, taught music at the Ospedale della Pietà, a Venetian orphanage. Its all-female orchestra was famous across Europe, and he wrote hundreds of concertos for them, including The Four Seasons.

title: The Grand Tour
text: Wealthy young Britons finished their education with a Grand Tour, travelling through Italy for months or years to see Rome's ruins and Florence's paintings. They shipped home so many souvenirs that Italian artists painted views especially for them.

title: Casanova's Escape
text: Giacomo Casanova was locked in the Piombi, the prison under the lead roof of the Doge's Palace. He broke out through the roof with the help of a monk in the next cell, then strolled out through the palace in the morning.

title: Pompeii Rediscovered
text: For centuries Pompeii lay forgotten under fields and vineyards. Excavations began in 1748 under the Bourbon kings of Naples. In 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli poured plaster into the hollows left by bodies, creating the famous casts.

title: Home for Foundlings
text: Florence's Ospedale degli Innocenti, designed by Brunelleschi, was one of the first hospitals in Europe for abandoned babies. Parents could leave infants in a revolving wheel at the door. Its arches are decorated with blue terracotta babies in swaddling.

title: Seeing With Sound
text: The priest and scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani noticed that blindfolded bats could still fly around obstacles, but deafened ones crashed. He couldn't explain how they did it; that had to wait until the 1930s, when scientists discovered echolocation.

title: Frog Legs and Electricity
text: Luigi Galvani noticed that dissected frog legs twitched when touched with metal. He thought he'd found animal electricity. His rival Alessandro Volta disagreed, and their argument led to the battery. Galvani gave us the word galvanise.

title: Avogadro's Number
text: Amedeo Avogadro, a lawyer turned physicist in Turin, suggested that equal volumes of gas hold equal numbers of molecules. Few believed him in his lifetime. Today every chemistry student learns Avogadro's number.

title: The Mathematician of Milan
text: Maria Gaetana Agnesi wrote one of the first calculus textbooks, and the first by a woman. A curve she studied became known in English as the Witch of Agnesi, thanks to a mistranslation of the Italian word for it.

title: The First Woman Professor
text: Laura Bassi earned a doctorate from the University of Bologna at 20 and became the first woman in Europe to be paid as a university professor. She taught physics for decades and ran experiments in a laboratory in her own home.

title: Napoleon's Iron Crown
text: Napoleon crowned himself King of Italy in Milan's cathedral with the Iron Crown of Lombardy, said to contain a nail from the True Cross. He reportedly declared, 'God gave it to me; beware whoever touches it.'

title: Exile on Elba
text: After his defeat in 1814, Napoleon was sent to rule the little island of Elba. In ten months he built roads and reorganised the mines, then slipped away by boat and landed in France, beginning his last Hundred Days.

title: Viva Verdi!
text: Patriots chalked 'Viva VERDI' on walls across northern Italy. It cheered the composer, but it was also code: Vittorio Emanuele Re d'Italia, Victor Emmanuel King of Italy. The chorus 'Va, pensiero' from Nabucco became an unofficial anthem.

title: The Composer Who Loved Food
text: Gioachino Rossini wrote The Barber of Seville in about three weeks. After his opera William Tell in 1829, aged 37, he stopped writing operas and devoted much of his time to cooking and eating. Tournedos Rossini is named after him.

title: The Unfinished Turandot
text: Puccini died before finishing Turandot. At its premiere at La Scala, the conductor Arturo Toscanini stopped where Puccini had stopped writing, turned to the audience and said, more or less, 'Here the maestro laid down his pen.'

title: La Scala Opens
text: Milan's opera house was built on the site of a church called Santa Maria alla Scala, which gave it its name. It opened in 1778 with an opera by Antonio Salieri, and its season still opens each year on 7 December, the feast of Milan's patron saint.

title: The Phoenix Rises Again
text: Venice's opera house is called La Fenice, the Phoenix, because it had already risen from fire once. It burned again in 1996 and was rebuilt exactly as it was, reopening in 2003. Verdi premiered Rigoletto and La Traviata there.

title: Garibaldi's Biscuit
text: Giuseppe Garibaldi fought for freedom in South America before uniting Italy, and became a hero in Britain too. A British biscuit full of currants was named after him. He spent his last years farming on the island of Caprera, off Sardinia.

title: Young Italy
text: From exile in Marseille, the Genoese patriot Giuseppe Mazzini founded Giovine Italia, Young Italy, a secret society dreaming of a united Italian republic. Members had to be under 40. Garibaldi was one of its recruits.

title: Through the Wall at Porta Pia
text: On 20 September 1870, Italian troops blasted a hole in Rome's walls near Porta Pia and entered the city, ending the pope's rule there. Rome became Italy's capital the next year, and many Italian towns now have a Via XX Settembre.

title: A Book Called Heart
text: Edmondo De Amicis's Cuore is the diary of a Turin schoolboy, full of stories about courage and kindness. Generations of Italian children read it at school, including the tale of a boy who crosses the ocean to find his mother in Argentina.

title: Millions Set Sail
text: Between about 1880 and 1915, more than four million Italians emigrated to the United States, most from the south. Millions more went to Argentina, Brazil and Australia. Today there are far more people of Italian descent abroad than in Italy itself.

title: Italians Down Under
text: After the Second World War, hundreds of thousands of Italians migrated to Australia. They brought espresso machines, delis and backyard vegetable gardens, and suburbs like Carlton in Melbourne and Leichhardt in Sydney became known as Little Italy.

title: Building the Snowy Scheme
text: The Snowy Mountains Scheme, which dammed rivers for power and irrigation in New South Wales, was built by workers from more than 30 countries. Italians were among the biggest groups, digging tunnels and building dams in the high country.

title: Prisoners on the Farm
text: During the Second World War, thousands of Italian prisoners of war were sent to work on Australian farms, often with little guard. Many got on so well with the farming families that they came back to settle after the war.

title: A Woman Runs the Paper
text: The journalist and novelist Matilde Serao co-founded the Naples daily Il Mattino in 1892. In 1904 she launched her own paper, Il Giorno, becoming the first woman in Italy to found and edit a daily newspaper. She was nominated for the Nobel Prize several times.

title: The Constitution
text: Italy's constitution came into force on 1 January 1948. Its very first article says Italy is a democratic republic founded on work. It has been amended many times since but is still the country's founding law.

title: Twenty Regions
text: Italy is divided into twenty regions, from Valle d'Aosta in the Alps to Sicily in the south. Five of them, including Sardinia and Trentino-Alto Adige, have special self-government, partly because of their islands, borders or minority languages.

title: The Little Mouse and the 500
text: Fiat's tiny 1936 Topolino, 'little mouse', put Italians on four wheels. Its successor, the Nuova 500 of 1957, was just under three metres long, and families squeezed into it for holidays all over the country.

title: The Lambretta
text: The Vespa's great rival, the Lambretta, was made by Innocenti in Milan and named after the Lambro, the river that flows past the factory. In the 1960s both scooters became favourites of the British Mods.

title: A Company Town With a Heart
text: Adriano Olivetti ran his family's typewriter firm in Ivrea as a model community, with libraries, nurseries, good housing and modern architecture for its workers. In 2018 the industrial town became a World Heritage Site.

title: Barefoot to Victory
text: At the 1960 Rome Olympics, the Ethiopian runner Abebe Bikila won the marathon running barefoot along the Appian Way, finishing by torchlight at the Arch of Constantine. He was the first black African to win Olympic gold.

title: Four Stars on the Shirt
text: Italy has won the football World Cup four times: in 1934, 1938, 1982 and 2006. The last came in Berlin after a penalty shoot-out against France. That's why the Azzurri wear four stars above their badge.

title: Football's Coming to Rome
text: Italy won the European Championship at Wembley in July 2021, beating England on penalties in a tournament delayed a year by the pandemic. The team brought the trophy home to Rome the next day.

title: The Cyclist Who Smuggled Papers
text: Gino Bartali, winner of the Giro and the Tour de France, hid forged identity papers in the frame of his bicycle on long 'training rides', helping to save Jews from the Nazis. He rarely spoke of it. Israel honoured him in 2013.

title: A Thousand Miles of Road
text: The Mille Miglia was a road race from Brescia to Rome and back, about a thousand miles. Racers sped through villages on public roads. It ended as a race in 1957, but lives on as a parade of classic cars.

title: The Temple of Speed
text: The Monza circuit, built in the royal park in just over 100 days, is one of the oldest motor-racing tracks in the world. It has hosted the Italian Grand Prix almost every year since, and Ferrari fans flood the track after the race.

title: The Mud Angels
text: On 4 November 1966 the Arno burst its banks and flooded Florence with mud and oil, damaging thousands of artworks and books. Young volunteers from around the world came to dig them out, and Florentines called them the angeli del fango.

title: Walls Against the Tide
text: The MOSE barrier, a row of 78 gates on the seabed at the entrances to the lagoon, was first raised against a high tide in October 2020. When the water rises, the gates fill with air and swing up to hold back the sea.

title: A Church on a Million Piles
text: Venice stands on wooden piles driven into the mud of the lagoon. The great domed church of Santa Maria della Salute, built to give thanks for the end of a plague, is said to rest on more than a million of them.

title: Saving the Leaning Tower
text: By 1990 the Tower of Pisa was leaning so far that it was closed to visitors. Engineers carefully drew soil out from under the high side, and by 2001 it had been pulled back by about 40 centimetres, enough for centuries more.

title: Bed After Carosello
text: Carosello was an evening TV show of short comic sketches, each ending with an advertisement. Italian children were allowed to watch it before bed, and 'dopo Carosello, a letto' (after Carosello, to bed) became a household rule.

title: The Sanremo Festival
text: Italy's great song contest has been held in the seaside town of Sanremo since 1951, and much of the country stays up to watch. It inspired the Eurovision Song Contest, and its winner often goes on to represent Italy there.

title: Volare
text: Domenico Modugno's 'Nel blu, dipinto di blu', better known as 'Volare', won Sanremo in 1958 and then topped the American charts, sung in Italian. It won the first-ever Grammy for Record of the Year, and Dean Martin's version made it a standard.

title: A Fistful of Dollars
text: Sergio Leone's westerns were made by Italian crews, often in the deserts of southern Spain, and became known as spaghetti westerns. Ennio Morricone's scores, full of whistles and twanging guitars, made them unforgettable.

title: Sophia Loren's Oscar
text: Sophia Loren won the Academy Award for Best Actress for Two Women, a film in Italian. She was the first person to win an acting Oscar for a performance not in English. She grew up poor in Pozzuoli, near Naples.

title: Benigni on the Chairs
text: When Roberto Benigni's Life Is Beautiful won the Oscar for best foreign-language film, he climbed over the seats in delight on his way to the stage. He also won Best Actor, the first man to win it for a performance not in English.

title: The Bicycle Thieves
text: Vittorio De Sica's film about a poor man searching Rome for his stolen bicycle used real streets and non-professional actors, typical of Italian neorealism. It is still regularly voted one of the greatest films ever made.

title: Italy's First Nobel for Literature
text: The poet Giosuè Carducci became the first Italian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1906. He taught at the University of Bologna for more than forty years, and his house there is now a museum.

title: The Writer From Sardinia
text: Grazia Deledda, who left school after four years and taught herself to write, won the Nobel Prize in Literature for her novels of life in rural Sardinia. She was only the second woman to receive it.

title: Golgi's Stain
text: Camillo Golgi found a way to stain nerve cells black with silver so they could be seen under a microscope. He shared the 1906 Nobel Prize for medicine, and a structure inside our cells, the Golgi apparatus, is named after him.

title: The Physicist Who Vanished
text: Ettore Majorana was a brilliant young physicist whom Fermi compared to Galileo and Newton. In March 1938 he boarded a ferry from Palermo to Naples and was never seen again. His disappearance remains a mystery.

title: Espresso in Orbit
text: In 2015 the Italian astronaut Samantha Cristoforetti made the first espresso in space, using a machine called ISSpresso built by Lavazza and an Italian engineering firm. She drank it from a special zero-gravity cup.

title: Morricone's Oscar
text: Ennio Morricone wrote music for more than 400 films and TV shows, from spaghetti westerns to Cinema Paradiso. Despite years of acclaim, he only won a competitive Oscar in 2016, aged 87, for Quentin Tarantino's The Hateful Eight.

title: La Dolce Vita in the Fountain
text: In Federico Fellini's La Dolce Vita, Anita Ekberg wades into the Trevi Fountain at night in a black evening dress. The scene was shot in winter and the water was freezing. Today, wading in the fountain earns a hefty fine.

title: Neapolitan Pizza Makers
text: In 2017 UNESCO added the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage, recognising the skill of spinning and stretching dough and baking it in a wood-fired oven.

title: The Fiat Factory With a Racetrack
text: Fiat's Lingotto factory in Turin was built with a test track on its roof. Cars were assembled floor by floor as they went up, then driven round the rooftop circuit. The building is now a shopping centre and the track is a garden.

title: Pirelli's Rubber
text: Giovanni Battista Pirelli founded his rubber company in Milan in 1872, making everything from telegraph cables to tyres. Pirelli tyres became famous in motor racing, and its Milan headquarters became one of Italy's first skyscrapers.

title: A Bakery in Parma
text: Pietro Barilla opened a small shop selling bread and pasta in Parma in 1877. His descendants turned it into the world's biggest pasta maker, still owned by the family and still based in Parma, where its factory turns out pasta day and night.

title: A Grocer's Coffee
text: Luigi Lavazza bought a small grocery shop in Turin in 1895 and began experimenting with coffee blends, an unusual idea when most people bought a single kind of bean. His family's company is still based in Turin.

title: The First Pizza in New York
text: Lombardi's, opened by Gennaro Lombardi in Manhattan's Little Italy, is often called the first pizzeria in the United States. Its licence dates from 1905, though Italian bakers there were probably selling pizza before that.

title: A Moustached Man on Every Stove
text: Alfonso Bialetti designed the Moka Express, an eight-sided aluminium coffee pot, in 1933. His son Renato marketed it with a cartoon of a little man with a moustache, and a Moka pot is now in almost every Italian kitchen.

title: Gucci Starts With Luggage
text: Guccio Gucci had worked at the Savoy Hotel in London, admiring the luggage of rich guests. Back in Florence in 1921 he opened a shop selling leather bags and travel goods, the start of one of the world's best-known fashion houses.

title: A Ducati Made of Radios
text: Ducati began in Bologna in 1926 making radio parts. After the war it sold a small motor, the Cucciolo, 'puppy', that clipped onto a bicycle. From there it went on to build some of the world's fastest motorbikes.

title: A Woman in the Speaker's Chair
text: Nilde Iotti, a teacher from Reggio Emilia who had fought with the partisans, was one of the 21 women elected in 1946. In 1979 she became the first woman to preside over the Chamber of Deputies, and held the post for thirteen years.

title: A Night at the Opera in an Arena
text: To mark 100 years since Verdi's birth, his opera Aida was staged inside Verona's Roman arena in 1913. The festival has been held there most summers since, with audiences of thousands holding candles as the sun goes down.

title: Turin's Winter Games
text: Turin hosted the Winter Olympics in 2006, with the ski events in the mountains above the city. Twenty years later, Milan and Cortina d'Ampezzo shared the 2026 Winter Games, the first officially hosted by two cities.

title: Liberation Day
text: On 25 April 1945, partisan forces called a general uprising in the cities of northern Italy as the Allies advanced. The date is now Liberation Day, a national holiday, often marked by singing the partisan song 'Bella ciao'.

title: The Mondiali Night of 1982
text: When Italy beat West Germany 3–1 in the 1982 World Cup final, the president, Sandro Pertini, aged 85, leapt from his seat in the stands. On the plane home he played cards with the players, the trophy on the table between them.

title: Pouring Onto the Track
text: The Mugello circuit in the Tuscan hills hosts the Italian motorcycle Grand Prix, one of the loudest days in Italian sport. Thousands of fans camp in the hills, and after the race they pour onto the track to the podium.

title: Italian Under Your Hand
text: Olivetti's Lettera 22, a portable typewriter launched in 1950, was light enough to carry anywhere and became the favourite of reporters and writers. One is kept in New York's Museum of Modern Art as a design classic.

title: The Birth of the Euro
text: Italy said goodbye to the lira on 1 January 2002, when euro notes and coins arrived; one euro was worth 1,936.27 lire. Each country chose its own designs for the coins, and the Italian one-euro coin shows Leonardo's Vitruvian Man.

title: Hundreds of Shapes
text: Italy has hundreds of pasta shapes, each suited to a different sauce: ridged penne to grip a thick sauce, long linguine for seafood, little orecchiette, 'little ears', for the turnip tops of Puglia. Many have several names, depending on the region.

title: Carbonara's Mystery
text: Spaghetti alla carbonara, now a Roman classic of eggs, pecorino, guanciale and pepper, doesn't appear in print until after the Second World War. One theory is that it grew out of the bacon and powdered eggs brought by American soldiers.

title: Alfredo's Fettuccine
text: Alfredo di Lelio made fettuccine with butter and Parmesan for his wife after she gave birth. Served in his Rome restaurant, the dish became famous when Hollywood stars Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks ate there on their honeymoon in 1920.

title: No Spaghetti in Bologna
text: In 1982 Bologna's chamber of commerce registered the official recipe for ragù alla bolognese, a slow-cooked sauce of meat, soffritto, tomato and milk. In Bologna it's served with tagliatelle or in lasagne, never with spaghetti.

title: Toni's Bread
text: One legend says panettone began when a kitchen boy named Toni saved a ruined Christmas feast in Milan by baking a rich bread with butter, sugar and raisins: pan de Toni. Whatever the truth, it's now eaten all over Italy at Christmas.

title: The Golden Bread of Verona
text: Domenico Melegatti patented pandoro, 'golden bread', in Verona in 1894. The tall star-shaped cake, dusted with icing sugar like snowy mountains, is panettone's great Christmas rival, and many families argue over which is better.

title: The Count's Cocktail
text: The story goes that Count Camillo Negroni asked his bartender in Florence to make his Americano stronger by swapping the soda water for gin. The result, equal parts gin, Campari and red vermouth, became the Negroni.

title: Harry's Bar Inventions
text: Giuseppe Cipriani of Harry's Bar in Venice created the Bellini, white peach purée with prosecco, and later carpaccio, thin slices of raw beef. He named both after Venetian painters, Giovanni Bellini and Vittore Carpaccio.

title: Ask for a Latte
text: Order a latte in an Italian bar and you'll probably get a glass of milk, because latte simply means milk. For the coffee version, ask for a caffè latte or a latte macchiato, 'stained milk'.

title: No Cappuccino After Lunch
text: Many Italians drink cappuccino only at breakfast, believing a big cup of hot milk after a meal is bad for digestion. After lunch or dinner, the done thing is a small espresso, drunk standing at the bar in a couple of sips.

title: Snow From the Volcano
text: Sicilians once collected snow from the slopes of Etna and stored it in stone pits to make frozen drinks in summer. Their granita, now made with lemon, almond, coffee or mulberry, is still eaten for breakfast with a soft brioche.

title: Cannoli for Carnival
text: Cannoli, crisp fried pastry tubes filled with sweet ricotta, were traditionally made in Sicily for Carnival. The best are filled just before you eat them so the shell stays crunchy, often topped with candied orange or pistachio.

title: Black Gold of Modena
text: True traditional balsamic vinegar of Modena is cooked grape must aged for at least twelve years in a series of smaller and smaller barrels of different woods. Families once started a set of barrels when a daughter was born, as part of her dowry.

title: A Town Named Gorgonzola
text: The blue cheese gorgonzola takes its name from a town near Milan where cowherds rested their herds on the way down from the Alpine pastures in autumn. It comes in two styles, creamy dolce and sharper piccante.

title: The White Truffle Fair
text: Every autumn, the town of Alba in Piedmont holds a fair for the white truffle, a knobbly fungus found by dogs in the woods. It's among the most expensive foods in the world, shaved paper-thin over pasta or eggs.

title: Sixty Million Olive Trees
text: Puglia, the heel of Italy's boot, has some 60 million olive trees, and produces more olive oil than any other Italian region. Some of its gnarled giants are thought to be well over a thousand years old.

title: Limoncello
text: Limoncello is made by soaking the peel of the big, fragrant lemons of Sorrento and the Amalfi Coast in alcohol, then sweetening it with sugar syrup. It's served ice-cold in small glasses after dinner.

title: The Black Rooster
text: Legend says Florence and Siena settled their border with a race: two riders would set off at cockcrow and draw the line where they met. Florence starved its black rooster, which crowed early, and won most of Chianti. The black rooster is now the wine's emblem.

title: Arancini or Arancine?
text: Sicily's fried rice balls are called arancine in Palermo and arancini in Catania, and the two cities argue about it endlessly. In the west they're usually round, in the east often cone-shaped, said to imitate Etna.

title: Focaccia for Breakfast
text: In Genoa, focaccia, a flat, oily bread with salt crystals on top, is eaten at any hour, including breakfast, when some people dip it in their cappuccino. Genoese bakers press their fingers into the dough to make its little dimples.

title: Pesto From Pra'
text: Pesto alla genovese is made by pounding basil, pine nuts, garlic, cheese and olive oil in a marble mortar; pesto comes from pestare, to pound. Genoa's prized small-leaved basil is grown in Pra', a district by the sea.

title: Golden Risotto
text: A legend says risotto alla milanese was invented when a glassmaker's apprentice working on Milan cathedral's windows added saffron, used to colour glass, to the rice at his master's daughter's wedding. Whatever the truth, it's been golden ever since.

title: Shaped Like Venus
text: A legend from near Bologna says an innkeeper glimpsed the goddess Venus asleep and was so struck by her navel that he shaped pasta like it: the tortellino. Bologna and Modena still argue over who makes the best, served in broth.

title: Polenta Before Corn
text: Italians ate polenta, a porridge of ground grain, long before maize arrived from the Americas. It was once made from barley, spelt or chestnut flour. Once corn spread in the 1500s, yellow polenta became the everyday food of the north.

title: Spritz in Padua
text: The Barbieri brothers launched Aperol, an orange-red bitter aperitif, in Padua in 1919. Mixed with prosecco and soda water, it makes the Aperol spritz, now drunk at aperitivo time all over Italy and far beyond.

title: Campari's Red
text: Gaspare Campari created his bitter red aperitif in Novara in 1860, then moved to Milan. His son Davide opened a bar in the Galleria and commissioned famous artists to design striking posters for the drink.

title: Breadsticks for a Duke
text: Grissini, Turin's thin crunchy breadsticks, are said to have been created by a court baker for the sickly young Duke Victor Amadeus II, who couldn't digest ordinary bread. Napoleon reportedly loved them too.

title: The Oldest Lasagne
text: Recipes for lasagne appear in Italian cookbooks of the 1300s, layered with cheese and spices. Tomato didn't join until much later. In Naples, lasagne is the great Carnival dish, layered with little meatballs, sausage and ricotta.

title: Neapolitan Coffee for a Stranger
text: In Naples, someone in a good mood might pay for two coffees and drink only one, leaving a caffè sospeso, a 'suspended coffee', for a stranger who can't afford one. The custom has spread to cafés around the world.

title: A Saint's Custard
text: Zabaglione is a warm custard of egg yolks, sugar and Marsala wine, whisked over hot water until frothy. Turin's version is linked to a Franciscan friar, San Pasquale Baylón, patron saint of cooks.

title: Parma Ham's Salt and Air
text: Prosciutto di Parma is made with just pork legs and sea salt, then left to cure for at least a year in the breezy hills south of Parma. Hams that pass inspection are branded with the five-pointed ducal crown.

title: Fruit Made of Almonds
text: Legend says the nuns of Palermo's Martorana convent, wanting to impress a visiting archbishop in autumn, hung their bare orchard trees with fruit sculpted from almond paste. Frutta martorana, painted to look real, is still made for All Souls' Day.

title: Mozzarella in Carrozza
text: Mozzarella in carrozza, 'in a carriage', is a sandwich of mozzarella dipped in egg and fried until golden. The cheese is the passenger and the bread is the carriage. It's a classic Neapolitan way to use up stale bread.

title: Pizza Bianca Romana
text: Roman bakeries sell pizza by weight, cut with scissors from long trays. Pizza bianca, just dough, olive oil and salt, is a favourite mid-morning snack, sometimes split and filled with mortadella.

title: A Mortadella the Size of a Barrel
