text: Bologna's mortadella is a huge, silky pork sausage dotted with cubes of fat. In 1661 a papal decree set rules for how it should be made, one of the first food protection laws. Americans named their own lunch meat 'baloney' after the city.

title: Chocolate City
text: When cocoa was scarce, Turin's chocolatiers stretched it with ground hazelnuts from the nearby Langhe hills. The result was gianduja, and from it came the gianduiotto, a little boat-shaped chocolate wrapped in foil.

title: The Bicerin
text: Turin's bicerin is served in a small glass: hot chocolate, then espresso, then cream, not stirred, so you taste each layer. The Caffè al Bicerin, opposite the Consolata church, has served it since 1763.

title: Ossobuco
text: Ossobuco, 'bone with a hole', is a slice of veal shin braised slowly until tender, with marrow in the middle of the bone. In Milan it's served with saffron risotto and topped with gremolata, a mix of lemon zest, garlic and parsley.

title: Cacio e Pepe
text: Cacio e pepe is pasta with just pecorino cheese, black pepper and a splash of the pasta's cooking water, tossed into a creamy sauce. It's thought to have started as shepherds' food, made from things that would keep for weeks.

title: Fish on Christmas Eve
text: In much of southern Italy, Christmas Eve is a meatless feast of seafood: fried baccalà, clams with spaghetti, eel and more. Italian-Americans turned it into the Feast of the Seven Fishes.

title: St Joseph's Fritters
text: Italy celebrates Father's Day on 19 March, the feast of St Joseph. Bakeries fill with zeppole di San Giuseppe, rings of choux pastry topped with custard and a black cherry. Joseph was a carpenter, but legend says he sold fritters too.

title: Pistachios of Bronte
text: On the black lava slopes of Etna, the town of Bronte grows bright green pistachios so prized they're called green gold. They're harvested only every other year, and turned into pesto, cream and cannoli filling.

title: Amaretti From Saronno
text: Legend says a young couple in Saronno created amaretti, crisp almond biscuits, to welcome a visiting cardinal. Wrapped in pairs in colourful tissue paper, they're often served with coffee.

title: The Sfogline
text: In Emilia-Romagna, sfogline are the women who roll fresh egg pasta by hand with a long thin rolling pin, until the sheet is so thin you can see the grain of the wooden board through it.

title: Burrata's Creamy Heart
text: Burrata was created on a farm near Andria in Puglia, reportedly in the 1920s, to use up leftover scraps of mozzarella. A pouch of mozzarella is filled with stracciatella, shreds of curd soaked in cream, then tied shut.

title: Neapolitan Ice Cream
text: Naples was famous for sorbets and spumoni long before gelato shops spread across Italy. Neapolitan ice cream, with three coloured layers, is said to echo the colours of the Italian flag.

title: Trofie and Trenette
text: In Liguria, pesto is often served with trofie, short twists of pasta rolled by hand, or trenette, a flat pasta like linguine. The classic way is to cook chunks of potato and green beans in the same pot as the pasta, then toss everything in the pesto.

title: A Wine Called Brunello
text: Brunello di Montalcino was developed by the Biondi-Santi family in the late 1800s, using only Sangiovese grapes. It must be aged for years before release, and it became one of Italy's most celebrated wines.

title: The King of Wines
text: Barolo, made from Nebbiolo grapes in Piedmont, is called the king of wines and wine of kings, because the royal House of Savoy loved it. Nebbiolo is named after nebbia, the autumn fog that rolls over the vineyards at harvest time.

title: A Shipwreck and Stockfish
text: In 1432 the Venetian merchant Pietro Querini was shipwrecked in Norway's Lofoten Islands, where he saw cod being dried in the wind. He brought stockfish home, and baccalà alla vicentina is still a speciality of the Veneto.

title: A University for Gelato
text: Bologna is home to the Carpigiani Gelato University, where people from around the world learn to make gelato. Proper gelato has less air and fat than ice cream, and is served a little warmer, so the flavour is stronger.

title: Gnocchi on Thursday
text: Traditional Roman trattorias follow a weekly menu: gnocchi on Thursday, salt cod on Friday, tripe on Saturday. The rhyme 'giovedì gnocchi, venerdì pesce, sabato trippa' is still known all over the city, and many trattorias stick to it.

title: Five Lands
text: The Cinque Terre are five fishing villages clinging to the cliffs of the Ligurian coast. For centuries the easiest way between them was by boat or footpath. Farmers built thousands of kilometres of dry-stone walls to terrace the slopes for vines.

title: The Blue Grotto
text: Locals knew of Capri's sea cave, but they feared it was haunted. In 1826 the German painter August Kopisch swam in and described its glowing blue light. Visitors still enter by lying flat in small rowing boats to fit under the low entrance.

title: Four Hundred Bridges
text: Venice is built on more than a hundred small islands in a lagoon, linked by around 400 bridges. There are no cars at all; everything from groceries to ambulances travels by boat, and rubbish is collected by barge.

title: Why Gondolas Are Black
text: Venetian gondolas were once brightly painted and decorated. Laws against showing off, passed in the 1500s, are usually given as the reason almost all of them are now plain black. A gondola is still built by hand from eight kinds of wood.

title: The Colourful Houses of Burano
text: On the island of Burano in the Venetian lagoon, every house is painted a bright colour. A popular story says it helped fishermen find their way home in fog. The island is also famous for its delicate handmade lace.

title: Letters to Juliet
text: Thousands of letters arrive in Verona every year addressed simply to Juliet. Volunteers of the Juliet Club answer them all. The famous balcony of 'Juliet's House' was actually added to the medieval building in the 20th century.

title: Mountains That Glow
text: At sunrise and sunset, the pale rock of the Dolomites turns pink, orange and purple, a glow called the enrosadira in the local Ladin language. The mountains became a World Heritage Site in 2009.

title: Closer to Africa
text: Lampedusa, Italy's southernmost inhabited island, is closer to Tunisia than to Sicily. Its Rabbit Beach, with turquoise water and white sand, is a nesting site for loggerhead sea turtles.

title: The Island of Long Lives
text: Mountain villages in Sardinia's Ogliastra and Barbagia regions have an unusually large number of people who live past 100, especially men. Researchers credit hard work, close family, a simple diet and plenty of walking up steep hills.

title: Mainland Europe's Only Active Volcano
text: Vesuvius last erupted in March 1944, during the Second World War, destroying dozens of American planes at a nearby airfield. Today some 600,000 people live in the danger zone around it, which is closely watched by scientists.

title: The Burning Fields
text: West of Naples lie the Campi Flegrei, the 'burning fields', a huge volcanic area with steaming vents and bubbling mud. The ground slowly rises and falls, and in the Roman market at Pozzuoli you can see marks left when the sea came in and out.

title: The Town on a Hill of Clay
text: Civita di Bagnoregio sits on a crumbling hilltop of soft rock, reached only by a long footbridge. Erosion has eaten away so much of it that it's called the dying town. Only a handful of people live there year-round.

title: The Mole of Turin
text: The Mole Antonelliana, with its tall, thin spire, was begun as a synagogue in 1863 and finished by the city in 1889. Once the tallest brick building in Europe, it now houses the National Cinema Museum, with a glass lift up the middle.

title: Spin for Luck
text: In Milan's Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, the mosaic floor shows the bull of Turin. Tradition says you'll have good luck if you spin round three times on your heel on a particular, very worn, part of the bull.

title: Naples Under Naples
text: Beneath Naples lies a maze of tunnels and caverns cut into the soft tufa rock, first quarried by the ancient Greeks. Later used as cisterns, they sheltered Neapolitans from bombing raids during the Second World War.

title: The Street of Nativity Scenes
text: On Naples' Via San Gregorio Armeno, workshops make figures for Christmas cribs all year round. Alongside the shepherds and angels you'll find pizzaiuoli, fishmongers, footballers and politicians.

title: The Talking Statue
text: A battered ancient statue near Piazza Navona, nicknamed Pasquino, has had anonymous verses mocking popes and politicians stuck to it since the 1500s. These satirical notes gave us the word pasquinade, and Romans still pin them there.

title: The Keyhole of Rome
text: On the Aventine Hill, people queue to peer through the keyhole of a green door belonging to the Knights of Malta. Through it you see a garden avenue framing the dome of St Peter's. Romans like to say you're looking at three states at once.

title: Learned, Fat and Red
text: Bologna has three nicknames: la dotta, the learned, for its ancient university; la grassa, the fat, for its rich food; and la rossa, the red, for its terracotta roofs and its left-wing politics.

title: The City of Bicycles
text: Ferrara, ruled for centuries by the Este family, is ringed by nine kilometres of Renaissance walls topped with a tree-lined path. It's so flat and bike-friendly that it's known as Italy's city of bicycles.

title: Oil From Florence
text: Dante died in exile in Ravenna in 1321, and Florence has been trying to get him back ever since. As a sort of apology, Florence sends the olive oil that burns in the lamp at his tomb in Ravenna.

title: Giotto's Blue Chapel
text: Enrico Scrovegni paid Giotto to cover the inside of his family chapel in Padua with frescoes of the lives of Mary and Jesus, under a ceiling of deep blue scattered with gold stars. It changed the course of European painting.

title: The Duke's Ideal City
text: Federico da Montefeltro, a soldier-for-hire who lost an eye in a tournament, built a palace and court of learning in hilltop Urbino. Raphael was born there in 1483, and his father worked at the duke's court.

title: A Park on the Walls
text: Lucca's massive Renaissance walls were built to keep enemies out but never needed for a battle. Today their tree-lined top is a four-kilometre park where locals walk, jog and cycle. The composer Puccini was born in the town.

title: The Longest River
text: The Po is Italy's longest river, flowing about 650 kilometres from the Alps to the Adriatic. Its wide valley is Italy's breadbasket, with rice paddies, maize and the dairy farms that make Parmesan.

title: Italy's Biggest Lake
text: Lake Garda is Italy's largest lake, so big that it has a mild climate with olive groves and lemon houses on its shores. Its northern end is surrounded by mountains, and steady winds make it a favourite for windsurfers.

title: Twenty-One Letters
text: The Italian alphabet has just 21 letters. J, K, W, X and Y are only used in foreign words, like jeans, kiwi and whisky. That's why Italians spell out Juventus with a letter they call 'i lunga', long i.

title: Days of the Planets
text: Most Italian weekdays are named after the Roman gods of the planets: lunedì for the Moon, martedì for Mars, mercoledì for Mercury, giovedì for Jupiter, venerdì for Venus. Sabato comes from the Sabbath and domenica means the Lord's day.

title: The Good Witch
text: On the night of 5 January, the Befana, a kindly old witch on a broomstick, brings sweets to good children and lumps of coal to naughty ones. Families leave out a glass of wine and something to eat for her.

title: Unlucky Seventeen
text: In Italy the unlucky number isn't 13 but 17. In Roman numerals it's XVII, which can be rearranged as VIXI, Latin for 'I have lived', meaning 'I am dead'. Some Italian hotels and planes skip row or room 17.

title: Numbers That Mean Things
text: In Naples, every number from 1 to 90 has a meaning in the smorfia, a sort of dream dictionary for the lottery: 33 is Christ's age, 77 is a woman's legs, 90 is fear. Neapolitans play tombola with it at Christmas.

title: Football in Costume
text: Calcio storico, a rough mix of football, rugby and wrestling, is played every June in Piazza Santa Croce by teams from Florence's four old quarters. In 1530, Florentines played a match even while their city was under siege.

title: Name Days
text: Many Italians celebrate their onomastico, the feast day of the saint they're named after, as well as their birthday. Every Giuseppe gets good wishes on 19 March, and every Francesco on 4 October.

title: Italian in Switzerland
text: Italian is an official language in Switzerland, spoken in the canton of Ticino and parts of Graubünden, as well as in San Marino and Vatican City. Swiss banknotes are printed in Italian alongside German, French and Romansh.

title: A Language of Its Own
text: Neapolitan is so different from standard Italian that UNESCO lists it as a language. It gave the world songs like 'O sole mio' and 'Funiculì, funiculà', the second written in 1880 for the new funicular railway up Vesuvius.

title: The Gesture Language
text: Italians are famous for talking with their hands. Fingertips pinched together and shaken means 'what do you want?' or 'what are you saying?'. In 2020 it even got its own emoji, the pinched-fingers hand.

title: Briscola and Scopa
text: Italian card games use a 40-card deck with suits of cups, coins, swords and clubs, and regional designs from Naples, Piacenza, Sicily and more. Briscola and scopa are played in bars and kitchens across the country.

title: Calcio's Single League
text: Serie A, Italy's top football league, began as a single national league in the 1929–30 season. Before then, the championship was split into regional groups. Juventus have won it more times than any other club.

title: Venice's Floating Funerals
text: Napoleon ordered that Venice's dead be buried away from the city. Since then, the cemetery has been on the island of San Michele, ringed by cypress trees, and funeral processions travel there by gondola or launch.

title: Rome's Ancient Cats
text: Rome's stray cats are protected by law as part of the city's 'bio-cultural heritage'. Volunteers known as gattare feed them in ruins, parks and courtyards, and one colony lives among the temples of Largo di Torre Argentina.

title: The Little Train of the Bernina
text: The red Bernina Express starts in Tirano, in Lombardy, rolling right through the town's streets, then climbs over the Swiss Alps without using cogs, looping round a famous circular viaduct at Brusio. The line is a World Heritage Site.

title: The Giant of Sicily
text: Mount Etna, over 3,300 metres high, is the tallest active volcano in Europe, and its height changes with every eruption. The Greeks said the god of fire kept his forge beneath it. It became a World Heritage Site in 2013, and its ash makes the soil rich for vines.

title: Lemons on the Amalfi Coast
text: Along the Amalfi Coast, huge knobbly lemons called sfusato amalfitano grow on terraces cut into the cliffs, under wooden frames that shelter them from wind. Farmers once carried the crates up and down the steep steps on their backs.

title: The Little Republic Inside Italy
text: Surrounded entirely by Italy, San Marino has its own passports, stamps and coins. It's run by two captains regent, who change every six months. Its three towers on Monte Titano appear on its flag.

title: Lake Como's Villas
text: Lake Como is shaped like an upside-down Y. Its shores are lined with grand villas and gardens, many built by Milanese nobles, and the little town of Bellagio sits right on the point where the branches meet.

title: The Truffle Hounds
text: Truffle hunters in Piedmont, called trifolau, go out at night with specially trained dogs to sniff out truffles. Pigs were once used too, but they like eating truffles as much as finding them. The art of truffle hunting is UNESCO-listed.

title: Matera's Cave Churches
text: Around Matera, monks carved more than 150 churches into the rock, many painted with frescoes. The landscape looks so much like ancient Jerusalem that film-makers have shot Bible stories there, including Pasolini's The Gospel According to St Matthew.

title: The Palio of the Donkeys
text: Asti and Siena have horse races, but Alba holds a Palio degli Asini, a donkey race, said to have started as a joke at the expense of nearby Asti. The donkeys rarely go where their riders want, which is half the fun.

title: Racing Up the Candles
text: Every 15 May, teams in Gubbio race three huge wooden 'candles', each topped with a saint and weighing about 300 kilograms, up the steep slopes of Monte Ingino. St Ubaldo, the town's patron, always arrives first.

title: Oranges in Ivrea
text: Ivrea's Carnival ends with the Battle of the Oranges, when teams on foot pelt horse-drawn carts with oranges. It recalls a medieval uprising against a tyrant. Spectators wear a red hat to show they're not taking part.

title: Italy's First Railway
text: Italy's first railway opened in 1839 in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, running about seven kilometres from Naples to Portici, near the king's palace. Today high-speed Frecciarossa trains run from Milan to Rome in about three hours.

title: Ferragosto at the Beach
text: Around 15 August, most of Italy goes on holiday at once. Cities empty, shops close, and beaches fill with rows of umbrellas at stabilimenti, beach clubs where families rent the same spot every year.
